purpose: Additional adversarial context check requested by parent; this is not an independent review of my own finding.

checks.result: The opening statement uses older buildings, without defining a statutory Altbau class or cut-off year. The Fraunhofer ID 363 house dates from 1973, fifty years before the 2023 submission, and retains original external walls and windows. A 1990 roof insulation measure and 2009 bathroom radiator change must remain prominent; this is a partially improved older building, not an untouched or universally representative one.

Re-read the entire opening summary and section 2.4 across physical pages 6–7. The later section welcomes the simple heat-pump compliance route, lists cost, installation, noise and ground-source constraints, and requests planning to locate heat pumps where they can cover the full heat demand. It expressly envisages avoiding expensive hybrid systems. That contextual nuance should be acknowledged; it supports an interpretation of the opening exclusivity sentence as overgeneralised shorthand rather than any inference of intent. It does not expressly limit the opening sentence to an identified unrenovated subgroup.

Re-read Fraunhofer ID 363 physical pages 235–236, including the equipment list and temperature graph caption. The listed heat generators are a ground-source heat pump and electric resistance backup for space/water heat, with no gas/oil boiler. The measured heater-to-compressor electricity ratios are 0%/0%, not a general claim of zero backup capacity. The technical counterexample therefore addresses gas/oil-hybrid necessity, while preserving backup-capacity and partial-improvement caveats.

The 3 April 2023 09:06 draft section 71c accepts a heat pump that covers building heat demand; it does not impose a gas/oil hybrid requirement merely because a building is older. This legal point supports consistency with the addressed route, but the empirical measurement is the primary evidence against technical exclusivity.

assessment: Retain the narrowly framed provisional finding that the opening categorical gas/oil-hybrid exclusivity claim is overbroad. Do not convert one empirical counterexample into a claim that every old building can cheaply use a heat pump, that all site constraints vanish, or that hardship exceptions are unnecessary. The later nuanced discussion weakens any reading that the author denied all existing-building heat-pump use throughout the submission.
